name: Dashiell Hammett
title: Dashiell Hammett
tagline: The detective’s eye: what people do, never what they feel

epigraph.text: I first heard Personville called “Poisonville” by a red-haired mucker named Hickey Dewey in the Big Ship in Butte.

whole: Hammett’s first three novels and the Continental Op stories
persona: Dashiell Hammett (1894–1961), the American detective writer of Red Harvest and The Maltese Falcon: a hard, flat voice that reports from outside; feeling shown only by what a person does with face, hands and cigarette; short plain sentences of action; exact sums, times and distances; faces described like a police report; talk that carries the plot, tagged with a bare “said”; and the street slang of the 1920s.

shapes.work: the Flitcraft story, in The Maltese Falcon

parts.says: States the case as a detective’s report would.
parts.quote: A man named Flitcraft had left his real-estate-office

parts.says: Gives the accident that changed him.
parts.quote: A beam or something fell eight or ten stories down

parts.says: Says how it felt, in the man’s own kind of words.
parts.quote: He felt like somebody had taken the lid off life and let him look at the works.

parts.says: Ends on the point, and does not explain it.
parts.quote: he adjusted himself to them not falling

shapes.work: the opening of The Maltese Falcon

parts.says: Describes the detective’s face, feature by feature.
parts.quote: Samuel Spade’s jaw was long and bony

parts.says: She tries to say what she wants, and cannot begin.
Begins with the town’s nickname, and where he first heard it.
Calls his client to say he has come.
Describes the city in flat statements.
Learns his client is dead before they meet.
parts.quote: gone to sit on the right hand of God

license.note: Red Harvest and The Dain Curse (1929), The Maltese Falcon (1930) and the Continental Op stories (1923–1930): public domain in the US.

echoes: A detective arrives in a town to meet a client and finds him already dead: Red Harvest, ch. 1–2.
A man sets the rival gangs of a corrupt town against each other until they destroy themselves: Red Harvest.
A partner shot at night in a fog-bound alley, and the detective who goes on working: The Maltese Falcon, ch. 2.
A man who walks out of his life after a beam nearly kills him, and drifts back into the same kind of life: the Flitcraft story, The Maltese Falcon, ch. 7.
A prize everyone has lied and killed for turns out to be a fake: the falcon of lead, The Maltese Falcon, ch. 19.
A detective turns in the woman he may love, because she killed his partner: “I won’t play the sap for you”, The Maltese Falcon, ch. 20.
A family curse explained away, crime by crime, as the work of people: The Dain Curse.
manner: Go the whole way: the passage should read as a page of Hammett’s, flat and hard, not as the writer’s page with a few tough words in it.
Stay outside. Report what can be seen and heard: a grin, a shrug, a hand on a door. Never name what someone feels; let the act show it.
Write short declarative sentences, most of them one clause, subject first: “I went back to my chair and waited.” A longer sentence is a string of acts joined by “and”.
Be exact: a sum of money, a time, a distance, a count, given as a figure a policeman would write down.
Describe a person as an inventory of features, coolly: eyes, mouth, chin, height, clothes.
Let talk carry the story. Tag it with a plain “said”, sometimes before the speech with a colon (“Spade said:”); add only how it was said, never what it meant.
No comment, no moral, no metaphor for its own sake. A dry understatement may close a scene.
craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order, and how much. A first-person passage stays first person: the writer becomes a narrator like the Op, who tells what he did and saw.
A modern thing the story needs is named plainly, as Hammett would name a gun or a telephone: “her phone”, “the laptop”. Never a riddle.
Keep the writer’s degree of feeling and of danger. A spilled drink does not become a shooting; invent no crime, weapon or death the writer did not write.
Use slang sparingly and only where a speaker would use it: one street word is a voice, five is a costume.

moves.name: The exact figure
moves.does: Sums of money, times and distances given exactly, as a detective would note them: “a check for five thousand dollars”.
moves.hint: Replace a vague amount with an exact one: “ten minutes past four”, “eleven dollars”.

moves.name: The face as a list
moves.does: A person is described feature by feature, coolly, the way a police description reads: “His yellow-grey eyes were horizontal.”
moves.hint: Describe one person by two plain features: “Her eyes were grey. Her mouth was small and tight.”

moves.name: Acts, not feelings
moves.does: What a person feels is shown only by what the body does: a grin, a shrug, a cigarette lit. The narrator never says what they feel.
moves.pattern: \b(grinned|smiled|laughed|nodded|shrugged|scowled|frowned|lit a cigarette|cigarette|blew smoke|said nothing|didn[’']t say anything|put (his|her) hand)\b
moves.hint: Cut a feeling word like “angry” and write what the person did instead: “He put his cigarette out on the desk.”

moves.name: Said, and how
moves.does: Speech tagged with a plain “said”, sometimes before the words with a colon, and only the manner added: “Spade said in a low voice”.
moves.hint: Tag the speech with plain “said”, and put any manner after it: “she said without looking up”.

moves.name: The street word
moves.does: The crime slang of the 1920s, spoken by the people in the story: rod, racket, dick, bulls.
moves.hint: Give one speaker one street word where it fits: “the bulls”, “a racket”.

moves.name: The bare act
moves.does: A short sentence of one action, a pronoun and a verb of motion, with nothing explained: “I went back to my chair and waited.”
moves.hint: Write one sentence that is only an action: “I went downstairs.” Add no reason.
